n: This psalm is a grand roll call of all creation, summoned to praise God. It begins at the very top—the heavens and the heights—and will work its way down to the earth.
The first worshippers called are the angels and the “hosts,” God’s heavenly armies. Even beings in God’s presence are invited to keep praising him.

f.g: hosts = armies, multitudes; here the angelic multitudes. “Lord of hosts” uses the same word.

n: Sun, moon, and stars are told to praise their Maker. Neighboring nations worshipped the heavenly bodies as gods; here they are only creatures giving glory to the true God.
“Heavens of heavens” means the highest heavens. The “waters above the heavens” reflects the ancient picture of the sky in Genesis, with waters above the firmament.

f.g: A Hebrew superlative: the highest heavens.

f.w: waters that be above the heavens

n: Why should all these praise God? Because they owe their very existence to him: he spoke, and they came into being.

f.w: he commanded, and they were created

n: God not only made the heavens but set them in fixed, dependable order. His laws for creation stand firm, a sign of his faithfulness.

f.g: stablished = established, set firmly in place.

f.w: a decree which shall not pass

n: Now the call turns to the earth, starting with the ocean depths and the great sea creatures. Even the creatures people feared most are part of the choir.

f.g: Hebrew tanninim—great sea creatures or sea monsters, as in Genesis 1:21; not the dragons of fantasy.

n: Weather is called to praise: fire (lightning), hail, snow, mist, and storm winds. Even wild storms are doing what God sends them to do.
The landscape joins in—mountains and hills, fruit trees and the towering cedars of Lebanon, the most prized trees of the ancient Near East.

f.g: Cedars of Lebanon, huge evergreen trees used for Solomon’s temple.

n: Every kind of animal is named: wild beasts, livestock, crawling creatures, and birds. The list follows the categories of the creation story.
Finally humanity: from rulers and judges down to all peoples. Those who hold power on earth are no exception—they too must bow before God.
Every age and gender is included—young men and young women, the elderly and children. Praise is not just for priests or the old; everyone has a voice.
The reason for all this praise: God’s name alone is truly exalted, and his glory is greater than earth and heaven together. All creation finds its purpose in honoring him.
The psalm ends with God’s covenant people. A horn symbolized strength; God has raised Israel’s strength, and they are “a people near unto him”—close to him by covenant.

f.g: A symbol of strength and victory, from the horns of a strong animal.
